summary: General case of adding and subtracting fractions with unlike denominators where neither denominator is a multiple of the other (e.g. 2/3 + 5/4), extended to mixed numbers (e.g. 3 1/4 − 1 3/5). Both fractions must be renamed to a shared unit — a common multiple of the denominators (twelfths for thirds and quarters) — which scales BOTH numerators, then like parts are combined. Mixed-number subtraction adds a further demand: the fraction part of the minuend can end up smaller than that of the subtrahend, forcing a regroup across the whole (borrow a whole) or a conversion to improper fractions. The unifying idea remains 'make the units the same, then count', now with no shortcuts.
misconceptions: Adds across the unlike denominators: 2/3 + 5/4 = 7/7, combining numerators and denominators.
Finds a common denominator but scales only one (or neither) numerator, or uses a wrong common denominator (2/3 = 2/12).

In mixed-number subtraction, subtracts the smaller fraction from the larger in each column regardless of position (does 12/20 − 5/20), never regrouping across the whole when the minuend's fraction part is smaller.

activities.title: Shared-grid combiner: rename both fractions, then combine
steps: Set up 2/3 + 5/4 on two strips or two number lines, one gridded in thirds and one in quarters, and notice they will not combine while the units differ.
Choose a shared unit (a common multiple of 3 and 4) and re-grid both strips into twelfths, re-tiling each fraction: 2/3 becomes 8/12 and 5/4 becomes 15/12.

State explicitly that cutting each third into four pieces turns 2/3 into 8/12 — the top is multiplied by the same factor as the bottom — and check the same for 5/4 (each quarter cut into three, so 5/4 = 15/12) before combining.
Combine the re-tiled pieces to get 23/12 and regroup into the mixed number 1 11/12.

Before computing, estimate: 5/4 is already more than 1, so adding a positive 2/3 makes the sum more than 1 (indeed more than 1.5). That already rules out answers like 7/7 = 1; the true sum lands just below 2 (23/12, just under 24/12).
activities.insight: Unlike fractions can only be combined once BOTH are rewritten over the same unit; each numerator scales by the same factor as its own denominator, and estimation gates whether a result is even possible.

activities.title: Mixed-number subtraction with a regroup across the whole
steps: Set up 3 1/4 − 1 3/5 and rename both fractions to a common denominator of twentieths: 3 5/20 − 1 12/20.
Notice that 5/20 is smaller than 12/20, so the fraction part cannot be taken directly — a regroup across the whole is needed.
Regroup one whole from the 3 into twentieths: break a whole tile into 20/20 so 3 5/20 becomes 2 25/20, then subtract to get 1 13/20.
As an alternative route, convert both mixed numbers to improper fractions first (3 1/4 = 13/4 = 65/20 and 1 3/5 = 8/5 = 32/20), subtract to 33/20, and convert back to 1 13/20.
Compare the two routes and decide which you find cleaner when a borrow is needed.
activities.insight: When the minuend's fraction part becomes smaller than the subtrahend's after finding a common denominator, you must regroup a whole into the common unit (or work with improper fractions) rather than subtracting the smaller fraction from the larger in each column.

activities.title: Explain and check with a model
steps: Work out 2/3 + 5/4 and 3 1/4 − 1 3/5, showing every step and giving each answer in simplest form as a mixed number where appropriate.
Explain how you chose the common denominator and why BOTH numerators changed when you did.
Answer the challenge: a friend says 2/3 + 5/4 = 7/7 = 1 — but 5/4 on its own is more than 1, so can the total be exactly 1? Explain what went wrong.
For the subtraction, after reaching 3 5/20 − 1 12/20, explain what you do because you can't take 12/20 from 5/20 as it stands.
Verify 23/12 against the benchmark: confirm it is more than 1 (since 5/4 alone exceeds 1) and a little less than 2 — does that match adding 2/3 and 5/4?
activities.insight: A learner secure in this strand can rename both fractions to a genuine common denominator, handle a mixed-number regroup by either route, simplify, and verify a result against a benchmark estimate — not just execute steps.

checkQuestion: Work these out, showing your steps: 2/3 + 5/4, and 3 1/4 − 1 3/5. Give each answer in simplest form, as a mixed number where appropriate.
